title: English 9
description: Free English 9 study guide: 8 units, 320+ practice questions, 80 flashcards, quick reference, memory tricks, and a full practice exam. Completely free.

units.name: Elements of Story

concepts.intro: Stories follow a shape: exposition → rising action → climax → falling action → resolution.
b: Exposition sets characters, setting, and the status quo the story will disturb
Rising action piles on complications — each conflict raises stakes
Climax = the turning point where the protagonist's fate tips; highest tension, not necessarily loudest scene
Falling action releases tension; resolution ties loose ends (denouement)
Not every story follows this line linearly — in medias res starts mid-action, flashbacks loop back

concepts.intro: Who tells the story controls what readers know and trust.
b: First person: I narrator — intimate but limited; everything filtered through one mind
Second person: you — rare, immersive (choose-your-own-adventure effect)
Third limited: outside narrator locked to ONE character's thoughts
Third omniscient: narrator knows everyone's inner life
Unreliable narrator: first-person voice whose account we suspect — irony engine

concepts.intro: Characters emerge through what they do, say, think, look like — and what others say.
b: Direct characterization: author states traits outright ('She was stubborn')
Indirect (STEAL): Speech, Thoughts, Effects on others, Actions, Looks
Protagonist drives the plot; antagonist opposes — not always a villain, sometimes nature or self
Flat vs round: flat = one trait; round = complex, capable of surprise
Static vs dynamic: dynamic characters CHANGE by the end — arc is the point

concepts.intro: Every plot runs on conflict; four classic engines.
b: Person vs person: the visible duel (rival, villain, sibling)
Person vs self: internal war — fear, guilt, addiction; often the deepest arc
Person vs society: laws, norms, institutions press on an individual
Person vs nature/fate: survival against storm, disease, destiny

keyFacts: Climax = turning point, not 'most exciting moment' by volume
Third limited = one head; omniscient = all heads
Dynamic characters change; static ones reveal the world around them
traps: Climax ≠ ending — resolutions come AFTER the climax
Antagonist isn't automatically evil; it's whatever blocks the protagonist
First-person narrators can lie or misread — don't equate narrator with author

units.name: Figurative Language & Literary Devices

concepts.intro: Simile, metaphor, and personification trade literal language for imaginative force.
b: Simile compares WITH like/as: 'Brave as a lion'
Metaphor compares WITHOUT: 'Time is a thief' — asserts identity
Extended metaphor runs across a whole passage/poem (allegory lives here)
Personification gives human traits to non-human: 'The wind whispered'
Implied metaphor skips naming one side: 'She sailed through exams'

concepts.intro: Poets and prose stylists pattern sound to make language memorable.
b: Alliteration: repeated initial consonants ('Peter Piper')
Assonance: repeated vowel sounds inside words ('the light of the fire')
Consonance: repeated consonant sounds ('pitter-patter')
Onomatopoeia: words that imitate sound (buzz, crash)
Hyperbole = deliberate exaggeration ('I've told you a million times')

concepts.intro: Irony lives in the gap between expectation and reality.
b: Verbal irony: saying the opposite of meaning ('Lovely weather' in a storm)
Situational irony: outcome contradicts expectation (fire station burns down)
Dramatic irony: AUDIENCE knows what character doesn't — horror and tragedy fuel it
Sarcasm = bitter verbal irony aimed at someone

concepts.intro: References and recurring images deepen theme.
b: Allusion: brief reference to myth, Bible, history ('He's a real Romeo')
Symbol: object standing for bigger idea (dove → peace); concrete carrying abstract
Motif: recurring image/idea that gains meaning through repetition
A symbol appears once possible; a motif MUST recur

keyFacts: Simile uses like/as; metaphor doesn't — that's the whole test
Dramatic irony = reader knows, character doesn't
Symbol once vs motif repeats — recurrence defines motif
traps: 'The rain cried' is personification, NOT pathetic fallacy confusion — keep terms precise
Hyperbole isn't meant literally — flagging it as a 'lie' misses the point
Verbal irony ≠ coincidence: situational irony needs expectation violated

units.name: Symbolism, Theme & Motif

concepts.intro: Theme is the argument a story makes about life — a full idea, not one word.
b: Theme ≠ topic: topic = 'love'; theme = 'Love demands sacrifice'
State themes as complete sentences about how the world works
Themes are debatable — evidence must support your reading
Multiple themes coexist; major + minor threads weave together

concepts.intro: Claims about theme stand on three-legged evidence: pattern, pivot, payoff.
b: Pattern: what recurs (images, phrases, situations) — motifs point at theme
Pivot: the moment characters realize/choose — thematic thesis lives in choices
Payoff: ending's consequence — what the story rewards or punishes
Formula to avoid plot summary: 'By doing X, the author argues Y'

concepts.intro: Common literary symbols and how context bends their meaning.
b: Water: baptism/rebirth — or drowning/danger; direction depends on treatment
Seasons: spring birth, winter death; autumn harvest or decline
Light/dark: knowledge vs ignorance, safety vs threat
A symbol means what THIS text earns — no symbol dictionary beats context

concepts.intro: Titles, frame stories, and endings encode theme deliberately.
b: Titles often name the central symbol or ironic phrase ('The Gift of the Magi')
Frame narrative (story inside story) contrasts values across tellings
Circular endings repeat an image changed by experience
Last lines reward rereading — authors plant theme in final sentences

keyFacts: Theme = full sentence argument; topic = single word
Evidence trio for theme essays: pattern → pivot → payoff
Symbols earn meaning from context, not from symbol dictionaries
traps: 'Love' is a TOPIC not a theme — theme must assert something about love
Don't hunt symbols first and force theme later; patterns emerge FROM reading
Motif ≠ symbol strictly: motif recurs; a symbol can fire once

units.name: Poetry Essentials

concepts.intro: Lines, stanzas, and fixed forms shape a poem before a single word lands.
b: Stanza names: couplet (2), tercet (3), quatrain (4), sestet (6), octave (8)
Sonnet = 14 lines: Shakespearean (ABAB CDCD EFEF GG) vs Petrarchan (octave+sestet)
Free verse abandons meter/rhyme — but still makes deliberate line breaks
Enjambment runs syntax past line end; caesura = pause mid-line

concepts.intro: Feet are stress-pattern bricks; iambic is English's native beat.
b: Iamb = unstressed-STRESSED (da-DUM): 'Shall I comPARE thee…'
Trochee reversed (DUM-da); anapest (da-da-DUM); dactyl (DUM-da-da)
Measure by count: pentameter = five feet per line — iambic pentameter = 10 syllables
Spondee (STRESS-STRESS) slows lines for weight

concepts.intro: Rhyme maps a poem's skeleton with letters.
b: Mark rhyme ABAB by end-sounds; slant rhyme is near-rhyme ('worm/form')
Internal rhyme sits INSIDE lines; rhyme scheme reveals stanza logic
Couplets snap conclusions — Shakespeare's sonnets argue then flip in the final couplet
Refrain returns whole lines like choruses — villanelles live on repetition

concepts.intro: Every poem has a constructed voice, distinct from the poet.
b: Speaker ≠ author always — dramatized voices, personas, monologues
Tone = speaker's attitude; diction and imagery carry it
Shifts (volta!) mark turns: sonnet volta arrives at line 9 or the couplet
Ask: who speaks, to whom, under what circumstances, wanting what?

keyFacts: Iambic pentameter = 5 iambs = 10 syllables, da-DUM × 5
Shakespearean sonnet: 14 lines, ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, volta often in couplet
Speaker ≠ poet — analyze the constructed voice
traps: Free verse isn't formless — line breaks and stanzas still make meaning
Rhyme SCHEME letters track END sounds only, not internal rhymes
The volta is a TURN in thought, not just another line

units.name: The Epic & The Odyssey

concepts.intro: Epic poems share a toolkit: invocation, epithets, vast scope, divine machinery.
b: Invocation: poet calls on a Muse to tell the story (Sing through me…)
In medias res: action starts mid-journey; backstory arrives via flashback
Epithet: recurring tag phrases — 'rosy-fingered Dawn,' 'Odysseus of many wiles'
Epic simile: extended comparisons running several lines, elevating the moment

concepts.intro: Odysseus's route maps the classic monomyth arc.
b: Call & refusal/launch → trials at sea (Lotus, Cyclops, Circe, Sirens, Scylla)
Underworld visit = descent and knowledge gained (Tiresias's prophecy)
Homecoming disguise/test phase — Odysseus returns as beggar to test loyalty
Return/restoration: reclaiming home, restoring order, reunions earned

concepts.intro: Each trial tests a different virtue or flaw.
b: Cyclops Polyphemus: wit over strength ('Nobody' trick) but hubris in shouting his name — curse follows
Sirens: temptation of knowledge/past; binding to mast = discipline beats desire
Scylla & Charybdis: impossible choices — sacrifice some crew to save the ship
Suitors & the bow test: identity proven through competence only he possesses

concepts.intro: Hospitality is the epic's moral operating system.
b: Xenia = guest-host law: hosts feed/gift guests BEFORE asking names
Violations of xenia draw punishment: suitors' doom is moral, not just plot
Kleos (glory/fame) motivates heroes — reputation outlives life
Nostos = homecoming song — the Odyssey IS the great nostos poem

keyFacts: In medias res + invocation + epithets = instant epic markers
Xenia violations drive the plot's justice: the suitors die for breaking hospitality
Epithets aid oral memory: 'wine-dark sea,' 'clever Odysseus'
traps: The Odyssey doesn't begin with Odysseus — it opens on Telemachus (the Telemachy)
Hubris means overreaching pride against gods' order, not just 'confidence'
Aeolus's wind bag fails because the CREW opens it — distrust, not Odysseus's sleep alone

units.name: Rhetoric & Persuasion

concepts.intro: Aristotle's three appeals still structure every argument you'll read.
b: Ethos: credibility — credentials, experience, fair tone, shared values
Pathos: emotion — stories, vivid images, fear/hope/pride activation
Logos: logic — facts, statistics, syllogisms, cause-effect chains
Strong arguments braid all three; pure logos can feel cold, pure pathos manipulative

concepts.intro: Arguments build from a debatable claim down through support.
b: Claim must be ARGUABLE — reasonable people could disagree
Reasons = mini-claims explaining why the claim holds
Evidence types: facts/stats, expert testimony, examples/anecdotes, analogies
Warrant: the unstated link between evidence and claim — make it explicit

concepts.intro: Strong writers invite the opposition in — then answer it.
b: Address the strongest counterargument, not a strawman
Concede where true ('It's true that costs rise…'), then pivot ('…but the long-term…')
Rebuttal structure: they say → but → because (evidence) → so
Refuting weak versions of opponents' views backfires with informed readers

concepts.intro: Ads, speeches, and op-eds deploy repeatable moves worth naming.
b: Rhetorical question: plants your conclusion as the audience's own thought
Anaphora: repeated openers build momentum ('We shall fight… we shall fight')
Tricolon: three-part lists feel complete ('life, liberty, and the pursuit…')
Loaded language: word choice smuggling judgment ('reform' vs 'gut')

keyFacts: Ethos = credibility · pathos = emotion · logos = logic
Claim → reasons → evidence → warrant: make the unstated link explicit
Best rebuttals concede what's true, then outweigh it
traps: A counterargument isn't weakness — omitting it is
Pathos isn't automatically bad; unearned pathos is the problem
Correlation in 'evidence' isn't causation — watch for leap-in-logic logos

units.name: Grammar & Mechanics Essentials

concepts.intro: Independent clauses can stand alone; dependents cannot — that's the whole architecture.
b: Independent clause = complete thought: 'The bell rang'
Dependent clause starts with subordinator (because, although, when): 'Because it rained…'
Simple = 1 IC · Compound = IC + IC (fanboys) · Complex = IC + DC · Compound-complex = 2+ IC + 1+ DC
Avoid comma splices (IC,IC) and run-ons — fix with period, semicolon, or fanboy

concepts.intro: Six comma jobs cover 95% of real writing.
b: Items in a series (with Oxford comma for clarity): red, white, and blue
After intro elements: 'After the game, we ate'
Around nonessential appositives: 'My brother, a chef, cooks' — essential ones take no commas
Before fanboys joining two ICs; NEVER between verb and its object
With quotes splitting dialogue tags: 'I'm here,' she said.

concepts.intro: Possession vs contraction; subject vs object pronouns.
b: Singular possessive 's; plural ending in s takes just an apostrophe (the dogs' bowls)
Its = possessive; it's = it is — the classic trap
Pronoun case: I/he/she/they as subjects; me/him/her/them as objects
Compare formally: 'She's taller than I (am)' — the missing verb reveals case

concepts.intro: Subjects agree with verbs; pronouns agree with antecedents.
b: Intervening phrases don't change agreement: 'The box of nails IS heavy'
Indefinite pronouns: each/everyone/either = singular
They/them now standard for singular unknown gender reference
Shift avoidance: keep person and number consistent within sentences

keyFacts: Compound needs a comma + fanboy before the second IC
its = possessive / it's = it is
Subject-verb agreement ignores interrupting prepositional phrases
traps: 'Between you and me' — prepositions take OBJECT case; 'between you and I' is the hypercorrection error
Nonessential appositive commas change meaning: my sister Ann (essential) vs my sister, Ann (one sister only)
Fewer for countables, less for amounts: fewer calories, less sugar

units.name: Writing: Thesis, Evidence & Paragraph Craft

concepts.intro: A thesis is a specific, arguable roadmap — not a fact or announcement.
b: Weak: 'This essay is about social media.' Strong: 'Social media erodes teen attention by rewarding speed over depth.'
Formula starter: [Subject] + [your arguable assertion] + [because/reason frame]
Place at end of intro in timed essays; complexity can split across two sentences
Test: could a smart person argue the opposite? If not, it's a fact, not a thesis

concepts.intro: Body paragraphs are self-contained argument units.
b: Point: topic sentence stating THIS paragraph's mini-claim (links to thesis)
Evidence: quote/data/fact — introduced with context, never dropped naked
Explanation: YOUR analysis of how evidence proves the point — longest part
Link: closing sentence ties back to thesis / bridges to next paragraph

concepts.intro: Quotes serve your syntax; they never stand alone.
b: Integrate grammar-wise: She calls the sea 'a breaker of hearts,' framing…
Signal verbs vary: argues, suggests, admits, observes — avoid 'says' repetition
Cite properly per class style (page/line); ellipses trim middles honestly
Quote only what you'll analyze — paraphrase background, quote language worth weighing

concepts.intro: Intros hook then commit; conclusions land the significance.
b: Hook options: surprising stat, vivid scene image, provocative question (then ANSWER it)
Funnel shape: broad-but-relevant → narrower → thesis
Conclusions restate thesis in NEW words + zoom out to significance ('why this matters')
No new evidence in conclusions — synthesis, not surprise

keyFacts: Thesis test: could someone reasonably disagree?
PEEL = Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link — explanation is the longest block
Never drop a quote without introducing and analyzing it
traps: Plot summary ≠ analysis — every body paragraph must ARGUE something
'In conclusion…' announcements weaken endings; just conclude
Announcing a topic ('I will write about courage') isn't a thesis

quiz.q: The turning point of a story is the:
quiz.e: Climax tips the protagonist's fate — the point of no return.
Limited = locked to one head; omniscient sees all.

o: Mara gave her last dollar away.
quiz.e: Showing action lets readers infer traits — indirect (the A in STEAL).

quiz.q: A character who changes by story's end is:
quiz.e: Dynamic characters transform; static stay fixed.

o: A law or norm crushes an individual
quiz.e: Societal forces (laws, customs) are the opposing power.
Epic convention: begin mid-action, flashback later.
Direct comparison WITHOUT like/as = metaphor.
Assonance = vowel echo ('light of the fire').

quiz.q: The fire station burning down is:
quiz.e: Outcome contradicts expectation — situational.

o: Audience knowing what a character doesn't
quiz.e: Reader/audience knowledge gap powers dramatic irony.
Words imitating sounds = onomatopoeia.

quiz.q: A recurring image that accumulates meaning is a:
quiz.e: Motifs recur; symbols can fire once but motifs repeat.

quiz.q: 'Love' as a theme statement fails because it is:
quiz.e: Theme needs a full assertion: 'Love demands sacrifice.'

quiz.q: Best evidence trio for theme claims:
quiz.e: Recurring patterns, turning-point choices, ending consequences.
Seasonal cycle: spring birth, winter death — context can twist it.

quiz.q: What distinguishes a MOTIF from a symbol?
quiz.e: Recurrence defines motif; repetition builds meaning.
Story-in-story frames juxtapose perspectives and morals.
Penta = five iambs, da-DUM × 5.
Three quatrains + couplet = Shakespearean rhyme scheme.
Enjambed lines spill over — meaning carries across the break.

o: The constructed voice in the poem
quiz.e: Speakers are personas; don't equate them with the author.
Volta = the turn — often line 9 or the closing couplet.
'Sing in me, Muse' — the invocation launches epic narration.
Recurring tag-phrases = Homeric epithets, built for oral memory.
The 'Nobody' ruse blinds Polyphemus — but pride later reveals Odysseus's name, courting Poseidon's curse.
Sacred hospitality: hosts serve guests before asking names.
Heroes chase kleos — fame that outlives them. Nostos = homecoming.
Bound to the mast, Odysseus hears forbidden song and survives — discipline beats desire.

quiz.q: Citing your ten years of coaching experience is which appeal?
quiz.e: Experience builds credibility = ethos.

quiz.q: A statistic about dropout rates serves:
quiz.e: Data and reasoning = logos.

quiz.q: 'We shall fight on the beaches… we shall fight in the hills' uses:
quiz.e: Repeated clause openings = anaphora (Churchill).
Concede-and-pivot beats strawmanning informed readers.

quiz.q: The warrant in an argument is:
o: the unstated link between evidence and claim
quiz.e: Warrants connect evidence to claims — make yours explicit.

quiz.q: 'Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness' is a:
quiz.e: Three-part lists feel complete — the tricolon.
Subordinator makes it dependent — it cannot stand alone.

quiz.q: Fix the comma splice: 'It rained, we stayed home.'
quiz.e: Semicolon, period, or fanboy fixes spliced independent clauses.

quiz.q: Correct possessive for multiple dogs' bowls:
quiz.e: Plural already ending in s takes apostrophe only.
Agreement follows the head noun (box), not the intervening phrase.

quiz.q: Choose correct case: 'Between you and ___, this plan is risky.'
quiz.e: Prepositions take object case: between you and ME.
Indefinite pronouns like everyone are singular.

o: Schools should start later because teen sleep cycles demand it.
quiz.e: Specific + debatable + reasons attached = real thesis.
Your analysis of evidence earns the grade — explain most.

quiz.q: Best way to introduce a quote:
o: Integrate with context and a signal verb
quiz.e: Quotes need grammatical homes: She argues that '...'

o: restate thesis in new words + zoom to significance
quiz.e: Synthesize significance — no new evidence at the end.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly?
quiz.e: its = possessive (no apostrophe); it's = it is.

quiz.q: Signal verbs for quotes include all EXCEPT:
quiz.e: Vary signal verbs; repetition flattens voice.

quiz.q: A symbol differs from an ordinary object because it:
o: carries abstract meaning the text builds
quiz.e: Concrete thing + earned abstract weight = symbol.

o: line breaks, stanzas, and sound patterns
quiz.e: No meter doesn't mean no craft — form lives elsewhere.

quiz.q: Theme differs from topic because theme:
o: makes an arguable statement about life
quiz.e: Core literary/rhetorical concept.
Core literary/rhetorical concept.
Core literary/rhetorical concept.
Core literary/rhetorical concept.
Core literary/rhetorical concept.

quiz.q: Iambic pentameter line count of stresses:
quiz.e: 3 trochees
AABB CCDD EEFF GG
Core literary/rhetorical concept.
Core literary/rhetorical concept.
Core literary/rhetorical concept.
Core literary/rhetorical concept.
Style/mechanics principle.
Style/mechanics principle.
Style/mechanics principle.
Style/mechanics principle.
Style/mechanics principle.

quiz.q: The part of a plot that introduces characters, setting and the basic situation is the:
quiz.e: Exposition gives background before the conflict builds.

quiz.q: A character who stays essentially the same from beginning to end is:
quiz.e: Static characters don't undergo important change; dynamic ones do.

quiz.q: A narrator who knows the thoughts and feelings of every character uses:
quiz.e: Omniscient means all-knowing.

quiz.q: Hints about events that will happen later in a story are called:
quiz.e: Flashback moves backward in time; foreshadowing points forward.

quiz.q: A character whose traits contrast with the protagonist's, highlighting them, is a:
quiz.e: Foils sharpen our view of another character by contrast.

quiz.q: An unreliable narrator is one who:
o: Can't be fully trusted because of bias, limited knowledge or deception
quiz.e: Readers must question the narrator's version of events.

quiz.q: 'The wind whispered through the trees' is an example of:
quiz.e: The wind is given a human action.

quiz.q: 'Her smile was as bright as the sun' is a:
quiz.e: A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'.

quiz.q: 'I've told you a million times' is an example of:
quiz.e: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration.
An oxymoron pairs contradictory terms.

quiz.q: A reference to a well-known person, place, event or text, such as calling someone 'a Romeo,' is:
quiz.e: Allusions rely on shared cultural knowledge.

o: A speaker says the opposite of what they mean
The audience knows something a character doesn't
An outcome is the opposite of what's expected
quiz.e: Sarcasm is a common form of verbal irony.

quiz.q: Which is a complete theme statement?
o: Ambition can destroy the people it is meant to lift up.
quiz.e: A theme is a full, universal statement about life, not just a topic word or plot fact.

quiz.q: A motif is best described as:
o: A recurring element that develops a theme
quiz.e: Repetition across the text builds meaning.

quiz.q: In many stories, a journey symbolizes:
quiz.e: Physical journeys often mirror inner change.

o: A story in which characters and events stand for abstract ideas
A true account of someone's life
quiz.e: Animal Farm is a well-known political allegory.

o: The author's attitude toward the subject
quiz.e: Mood is the feeling created in the reader; tone is the author's attitude.

quiz.q: To support a theme claim in an essay, you should:
o: Cite specific textual evidence and explain how it shows the theme
quiz.e: Evidence plus explanation makes the argument.

quiz.q: A group of lines in a poem, like a paragraph in prose, is a:
quiz.e: A couplet is specifically two rhyming lines.

quiz.q: Two consecutive rhyming lines are a:
quiz.e: A Shakespearean sonnet ends with a couplet.

quiz.q: A line or phrase repeated regularly throughout a poem is a:
quiz.e: Refrains often appear at the end of stanzas.

quiz.q: A pause in the middle of a line of poetry is a:
quiz.e: It's often marked by punctuation.
The form comes from Japanese poetry.

quiz.q: A narrative poem is one that:
o: Expresses personal feeling without a story
quiz.e: Epics and ballads are narrative poems.

o: A larger-than-life figure who embodies the values of a culture
An ordinary person with no special traits
quiz.e: Odysseus represents Greek ideals like cunning and courage.

quiz.q: The Odyssey was traditionally attributed to:
quiz.e: Homer is also credited with the Iliad.

o: An extended, elaborate comparison over several lines
quiz.e: Also called a Homeric simile.

quiz.q: Odysseus's main goal throughout the Odyssey is to:
quiz.e: His nostos, or homecoming, drives the plot.

quiz.q: Penelope's unweaving of the shroud each night shows her:
quiz.e: She delays the suitors while waiting for Odysseus.

o: Excessive pride that leads to downfall
quiz.e: Odysseus's boast to the Cyclops brings Poseidon's anger.

quiz.q: An appeal to the audience's emotions is:
quiz.e: Stories and vivid images create emotional appeal.

quiz.q: A counterclaim in an argument is:
o: An opposing position the writer acknowledges and answers
quiz.e: Addressing counterclaims strengthens credibility.

o: A question asked for effect, not to get an answer
quiz.e: It prompts the audience to think.

quiz.q: Repeating the same word or phrase at the start of successive sentences is:
quiz.e: E.g. 'We shall fight… we shall fight…'.

o: Words with strong emotional connotations meant to sway readers
quiz.e: E.g. 'reckless scheme' vs. 'new plan'.

quiz.q: The purpose of a persuasive essay is to:
o: Convince readers to accept a position or take action
quiz.e: Persuasion combines claims, evidence and appeals.

quiz.q: Which sentence is a run-on (fused sentence)?
o: I finished my homework, and I went to bed.
I finished my homework; I went to bed.
After I finished my homework, I went to bed.
I finished my homework I went to bed.
quiz.e: Two independent clauses with no punctuation or conjunction.

o: There car is parked over their, and they're coming soon.
They're car is parked over there, and their coming soon.
Their car is parked over they're, and there coming soon.
Their car is parked over there, and they're coming soon.
quiz.e: Their = possession; there = place; they're = they are.

quiz.q: Choose the correct pronoun: 'My friend and ___ went to the game.'
quiz.e: It's a subject, so use 'I' (test it: 'I went to the game').

quiz.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
o: Because I love reading; I go to the library.
I love reading; my brother prefers movies.
quiz.e: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses.

quiz.q: 'Running down the hall, the bell rang.' This sentence has a:
quiz.e: The bell wasn't running; the modifier has no logical subject.

quiz.q: Which word correctly completes: 'The team ___ its first game.'
quiz.e: A collective noun acting as a unit takes a singular verb and pronoun.

quiz.q: A thesis statement should be placed:
o: In the middle of the essay
Usually at the end of the introduction
quiz.e: It tells the reader the essay's central claim early.

quiz.q: Which is the best topic sentence for a body paragraph?
o: Odysseus's cleverness helps him survive the Cyclops.
The Odyssey is a long poem.
In this paragraph I will talk about things.
quiz.e: It states one clear, arguable point the paragraph will prove.

quiz.q: After including a quotation, a writer should:
o: Explain how the quotation supports the claim
Move directly to the next quotation
quiz.e: Analysis connects evidence to the argument.

quiz.q: Transitions such as 'however' and 'furthermore' help to:
quiz.e: They guide readers through the logic.

o: Using someone else's words or ideas without credit
quiz.e: Always credit sources.

quiz.q: During revision, a writer should focus first on:
o: Big-picture issues like argument and organization
quiz.e: Fix structure before polishing sentences.

PART_B2.q: Unpack the symbolism: a wilting plant on a windowsill across three scenes most likely tracks:
o: a relationship's or hope's decline — and possibly revival at scene's end
PART_B2.e: Recurring object + placement near key moments = thematic barometer; the last appearance decides direction.

PART_B2.q: Distinguish the speaker's stance from the poet's in one sentence:
o: The speaker is a constructed voice; the poet authors it — stances may clash (ironist's mask)
PART_B2.e: Persona poems make the speaker/poet gap the whole point.

PART_B2.q: Which thesis BEST fits evidence about later school starts improving attendance?
o: Because teen circadian rhythms run late, delayed start times measurably raise attendance — districts should adopt them.
PART_B2.e: Specific claim + causal reasoning + policy payoff = full-strength thesis.

PART_B2.q: Name the device: 'Ask not what your country can do for you…'
PART_B2.e: Mirrored reversal of structure = chiasmus; also antithetical framing.

PART_B2.q: A director frames the Sirens scene with Odysseus straining against ropes. The shot argues:
PART_B2.e: Visual emphasis on restraint dramatizes the discipline-over-desire theme.

PART_B2.q: Fix and justify: 'Each of the players have a locker.'
o: have → has: 'each' is singular regardless of the plural noun that follows
PART_B2.e: Indefinite pronoun each takes singular agreement.

PART_B2.q: Why does Homer delay Odysseus's reveal until the bow test?
o: Identity proven through competence makes the reunion earned, not given
PART_B2.e: Narrative deferral converts recognition into justice.

PART_B2.q: Convert to formal register: 'Kids these days don't even read, which is super bad.'
o: Contemporary students read less frequently, a trend with measurable costs.
PART_B2.e: Formal register: precise nouns, hedged claims, no slang intensifiers.

PART_B2.q: Spot the faulty logos: 'Sales rose after our mascot change, so the mascot caused it.'
o: Post hoc reasoning — other variables uncontrolled

PART_B2.q: Choose the correctly punctuated complex sentence:
o: Although the storm passed, the harbor remained closed.
Although the storm passed the harbor remained closed.
The storm passed, the harbor remained closed.
PART_B2.e: Introductory dependent clause takes a comma; splice avoided.

PART_C.q: Synthesis: Using ONE epic convention and ONE rhetorical appeal, argue why The Odyssey remains taught today. Strongest answer:
o: Its in-medias-res structure (convention) still hooks modern audiences the same way ethos-laden retellings (appeal) borrow Homeric credibility — proving the toolkit endures because it works on human attention.
PART_C.e: Names concrete convention + appeal, then argues the causal link to enduring relevance — synthesis, not summary.

PART_C.q: Essay prompt: 'Fiction teaches empathy better than nonfiction.' Draft your thesis + PEEL skeleton. Best skeleton:
o: Thesis: Fiction builds empathy by simulating inner lives; P1 point: first-person POV trains perspective-taking + quote from a novel + explanation linking brain research; P2: literary counterargument conceded (facts matter) but outweighed; Link back.
Thesis: books are good. P1: reading. P2: more reading.
No thesis; list five novels I enjoyed.
Thesis: nonfiction is fake news; P1: opinions.
PART_C.e: Arguable thesis, POV-specific mechanism, evidence types named, counterargument conceded and outweighed — complete argument architecture.
